disputed.claim: that Taylor and Mason went through a form of marriage in 1893, Taylor in woman's dress as the bride, with an exchange of rings and a wedding breakfast
disputed.asserted_by: Charles Parker on oath at the Old Bailey, 26 April 1895 (Hyde p. 193); Pierre Louys to Andre Gide at the time, 'a marriage - a real marriage - between two of them, with an exchange of rings and so on'; Taylor himself, retold repeatedly and with laughter, per Croft-Cooke p. 143; and, obliquely, Wilde's own letters to Mason asking after his 'married life'
disputed.disputed_by: Taylor, on oath (Hyde p. 281), who denied that any marriage ceremony took place - while in the same testimony admitting that he slept with Mason 'the first night' and that he addressed him 'Dear Charlie. With love.'
disputed.grounds: The denial was made under criminal jeopardy, in a courtroom where the ceremony was being offered as proof of depravity, which is a reason to weigh it lightly - but it is a sworn denial by one of the two people concerned and it is not dropped. Scholars divide on what the event was: McKenna calls it a 'mock marriage service', Louys called it a real one, and the Complete Letters editors record Croft-Cooke's suggestion that it was genuine.

summary: In 1893 Alfred Taylor and Charles Spurrier Mason went through a marriage ceremony - Taylor in a wedding dress as the bride, Mason as the bridegroom, rings exchanged, a wedding breakfast for friends afterwards. Pierre Louys wrote to Andre Gide about it at the time; Taylor told the story afterwards himself, laughing; Wilde asked after Mason's 'married life' in a letter of about 13 August 1894. Charles Parker gave it in evidence against both men at the Old Bailey in April 1895, where Taylor denied on oath that any ceremony had taken place while admitting that he had slept with Mason 'the first night' and had written to him 'Dear Charlie. With love.'

sources.quote: Taylor told us on that occasion that he had gone through a form of marriage with a youth named Mason. Did he say who acted as the woman?—Yes; he said he did; that he was in woman's dress, and that they had a wedding breakfast.
sources.context: Charles Parker's examination-in-chief, Regina v. Wilde and Taylor, 26 April 1895
